title: Victory, Land, and a Refused Prayer
overview: Moses recalls defeating King Og, giving the land east of the Jordan to two and a half tribes, and being told he himself will never cross into the promised land.

parts.label: Victory over Og (vv. 1-7)
parts.note: Og ruled Bashan, a rich highland east of the Jordan River, and Israel defeated him as they had defeated King Sihon in the previous chapter. The text says plainly that they destroyed every town, killing men, women and children, and kept only the livestock and goods.

parts.label: The land and Og's bed (vv. 8-11)
parts.note: Israel now held the land east of the Jordan, from the Arnon gorge in the south to snowy Mount Hermon in the north, which neighboring peoples called by other names. Og is remembered as the last of the Rephaites, an ancient people pictured as giants, and his iron bed (some scholars think the word means coffin) was about 13 feet long and still on show in Rabbah, today's Amman.

parts.label: Dividing the eastern land (vv. 12-17)
parts.note: Moses gave this territory to the tribes of Reuben and Gad and to half the tribe of Manasseh, herding families who wanted its good pasture. Setting a border in the middle of the Arnon gorge may have been meant to prevent fights over water, and phrases like "to this day" suggest to many scholars that a later editor added notes.

parts.label: A promise to keep fighting (vv. 18-20)
parts.note: These tribes could settle their families and herds now, but their fighting men had to cross the Jordan and lead the other tribes into battle. They could go home only once everyone else also had land and "rest," meaning safety and a settled life.

parts.label: Courage for Joshua (vv. 21-22)
parts.note: Moses told Joshua, who would succeed him as leader, to treat the two victories he had just seen as a sign of what was coming. The core message is that the LORD would fight for Israel.

parts.label: Moses asks and is refused (vv. 23-29)
parts.note: Moses begged to cross over and see the land, but the LORD told him firmly to stop asking. He could only look at it from Pisgah, a high ridge, and was told to strengthen Joshua to lead the people in; here Moses links the refusal to the people, while Numbers 20 ties it to his own actions.

disagreement: Christians genuinely differ over how to read the total destruction of whole populations here, whether as literal history, as exaggerated ancient war language, or as Israel's later understanding of God that should not be taken at face value.
think: Moses could see the land he had spent his life leading people toward but could not enter it; how do you think about working for something you may never see finished yourself?
